query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing approximately 5 atomic percent titanium by substituting one of the constituent elements in equal-atomic NbMoTaW will improve room-temperature ductility by promoting local lattice distortions that ease dislocation motion and enhance grain-boundary cohesion, while maintaining the alloy’s high‐temperature mechanical strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent high-temperature strength but very limited ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Alloying by substituting roughly 5 at.% of one of the original elements (e.g., Nb) with titanium during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests at room temperature (to assess plasticity), at 1600 °C (to examine high-temperature yield/strength), and under irradiation conditions similar to those used in previous studies.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and the possible formation of nanoscale coherent regions that facilitate dislocation activity and improve grain-boundary cohesion.
generation.mechanism: Titanium addition lowers the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation and motion at room temperature by introducing controlled lattice distortions, without disrupting the overall BCC matrix that is critical for high-temperature performance and irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the pristine alloy, the Ti-doped NbMoTaW alloy is expected to exhibit a marked improvement in room-temperature ductility (increased strain-to-failure) while retaining comparable high-temperature strength (around 1600 °C) and similar resistance to irradiation-induced defects.
generation.baseline: Pristine equiatomic NbMoTaW, which is known for high high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance but suffers from poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only when the titanium substitution is kept near 5 at.%; higher additions or improper processing may lead to secondary phase formation that could compromise both high-temperature performance and irradiation stability.
generation.uncertainty: While preliminary evidence suggests titanium can enhance ductility through lattice distortion, the optimal substitution level and precise balance with high-temperature properties require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys using identical thermomechanical processing: one baseline NbMoTaW and one with ~5 at.% titanium substituting for Nb. Perform phase identification (e.g., XRD, TEM) to verify maintenance of the single-phase BCC structure. Evaluate mechanical properties through room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature (∼1600 °C) strength measurements, and conduct irradiation tests under controlled conditions.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength and creep resistance at ~1600 °C
Irradiation response assessed by defect density and changes in hardness
Microstructural analyses confirming phase stability and titanium-induced lattice distortions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-substituted alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility without a deterioration of high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance relative to the pristine NbMoTaW baseline, or if secondary phases appear after processing, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory HEAs (RHEAs) stand out among various types of HEAs due to their unparalleled mechanical properties at high temperatures exceeding 800 °C, and even up to 1500 °C in some cases [,], making them viable options for high-temperature structural applications, outperforming typical Ni-based superalloys. Refractory high-entropy alloys, thanks to their high strength at high temperatures, high melting point, and high hardness brought by their resistance to friction and wear properties, may be used in aerospace engines, gas turbines, and the nuclear irradiation field. However, the reported literature has primarily centered on compression deformation investigations. For most RHEAs, due to their room-temperature brittleness, their tensile ductility is commonly negligible []. Therefore, improving the room-temperature plasticity of RHEAs is the premise of its high-temperature application.

One such class comprises the RHEAs which, because of their high melting points, have been proposed as candidates for ultrahigh-temperature applications. However, a single-phase RHEA, TiZrHfNbTa, was recently shown to be significantly weaker in creep than CMSX-4 despite the former’s higher melting point. The weakness was ascribed to two factors: faster diffusion in the BCC matrix of the RHEA relative to the FCC matrix of CMSX-4 and a lack of precipitates. Additional research is therefore needed to enhance the creep strength of TiZrHfNbTa, for example, by the introduction of suitable strengthening precipitates. Meanwhile, RHEAs with higher melting points must also be investigated since diffusion will be slower in such materials. One such RHEA is VNbMoTaW, whose melting point is ~500 °C higher than TiZrHfNbTa,,. However, it has a major disadvantage: lack of ductility at room temperature even in compression. In contrast, TiZrHfNbTa exhibits ductility at room temperature both in compression and in tension (~8%), albeit not as much as the highly ductile and fracture-resistant FCC HEAs. The present work is the first demonstration of enhancing the ductility of high-strength BCC + B2 two-phase RHEAs by controlling their microstructure. For this, Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr was selected, based on its low density (7.4 g/cm3) and previous reports of excellent room and high temperature yield strength. This alloy was cast, hot isostatically pressed (HIPed) and then homogenized at 1200 °C for 24hrs followed by slow cooling (10 °C/min) to room temperature. The resultant microstructure consists of two BCC phases (one of which is likely ordered, but this was not previously proven) with very similar lattice parameters that form a very fine, inter-woven baskteweave-like, nano-phase structure. One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa []. On the other hand, these alloys are brittle at room temperature, leading to significant limitations of their application as structural materials. Later, in Reference [], it was shown that th

After the first development of RHEAs in 2010, over 150 kinds of compositions have been reported, with their potential for use in high-temperature applications such as gas turbine engines and rocket nozzles. Various studies focused on ductility enhancement [,], better oxidation resistance [], and nuclear reactor material applications [,]. According to a review by Senkov et al. [], the only alloys to pass high-temperature compression tests at 1600°C were MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW. The main reason for the difficulty to perform compression tests at extremely high temperatures is the lack of suitable material as a jig material that provides high strength at extremely high temperatures. Recently, Wang et al. strengthened the grain boundary of an MoNbTaW-refractory high-entropy alloy through doping with B or C in trace amount, which simultaneously increases room-temperature strength and toughness []. This study provides a good strategy to increase the ductility of RHEAs by doping suitable elements.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount (~5 atomic%) of titanium as a substitutional alloying element (e.g., replacing Nb) in the equal-atomic NbMoTaW will promote the formation of coherent, locally ordered regions that facilitate dislocation motion at room temperature, thereby improving ductility without compromising high‐temperature strength or irradiation resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Single‐phase BCC equal‐atomic NbMoTaW HEA that has excellent strength at 1600 °C and good irradiation resistance by first‐principles predictions but exhibits very poor room-temperature ductility.
drafts.intervention: Substitute approximately 5 atomic% of Nb with Ti during alloy processing to create a modified NbMoTaWTi alloy.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical tests performed at room temperature and 1600 °C, alongside controlled irradiation exposure experiments, under conventional thermomechanical processing conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The addition of Ti is predicted to induce nanoscale regions or coherent precipitates within the BCC matrix which act as local ductility enhancers (by providing sites for enhanced dislocation nucleation/motion) while maintaining overall lattice coherence.
drafts.mechanism: Ti has a lower elastic modulus and can lower the energy barriers for dislocation nucleation. Its substitution is expected to induce local short-range ordering or coherent secondary phase formation that aids in crack blunting and dislocation mobility, thereby increasing room-temperature ductility. Because the population of these regions is limited and coherent with the matrix, the high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance should not be significantly impaired.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the Ti-doped alloy will exhibit improved room-temperature ductility (e.g., increased strain to failure and higher toughness) while retaining the excellent 1600 °C strength and preserving irradiation resistance.
drafts.baseline: The unmodified equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy, which is strong at high temperatures and irradiation resistant but has poor room-temperature ductility.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis assumes that the Ti content is kept low (around 5 atomic%) to avoid excessive phase separation or formation of brittle intermetallic phases. Exceeding this doping level or improper processing that fails to achieve coherent precipitate formation could compromise high-temperature performance or irradiation tolerance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys based on NbMoTaW with varying Ti substitutions (e.g., 0%, 2.5%, 5%, and 7.5% Ti replacing Nb). Process the alloys under identical thermomechanical conditions and conduct microstructural analysis (using TEM, EBSD) to detect the presence of coherent precipitates or locally ordered regions. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to evaluate ductility, high-temperature mechanical tests at 1600 °C, and standardized irradiation experiments to assess defect accumulation.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile strain-to-failure and toughness metrics
Irradiation resistance evaluated by post-irradiation defect density and mechanical property retention
High-resolution microstructural characterization to confirm the formation and coherence of precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Ti-doped alloys (around 5 atomic% Ti) do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility without a concomitant reduction in high-temperature performance or irradiation resistance compared to the baseline NbMoTaW alloy.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small, controlled addition of a high-melting-point ductility‐promoting element (e.g., hafnium) into the NbMoTaW matrix will improve room‐temperature ductility by locally softening the BCC lattice (via lattice distortion that facilitates dislocation nucleation and motion) without significantly impairing its high‐temperature strength or irradiation resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW, a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties but poor ductility at room temperature.
drafts.intervention: Microalloying by substituting approximately 5 at.% of one of the original elements with hafnium (resulting in a composition such as HfNbMoTaW), ensuring the overall single-phase BCC structure is maintained.
drafts.conditions: The alloy should be synthesized and homogenized (e.g., via high-temperature annealing) under conditions that avoid the formation of secondary phases. Testing should be conducted at room temperature, at 1600 °C, and under irradiation conditions similar to those used in prior first-principles studies.
drafts.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortion induced by Hf addition, promoting dislocation activity at room temperature while retaining the high atomic packing efficiency and phase stability at 1600 °C.
drafts.mechanism: The Hf addition leads to moderate lattice expansion and increased local stress fields that lower the activation energy for dislocation motion at room temperature, thus increasing ductility. The high melting point and refractory nature of Hf help ensure that the high-temperature performance is not compromised, and the single-phase BCC structure preserves the characteristics related to irradiation resistance predicted in the original NbMoTaW system.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline, the Hf-doped alloy is expected to show improved room-temperature ductility with a lower yield strength (indicating easier plasticity initiation) while maintaining similar high-temperature mechanical performance at 1600 °C and comparable irradiation resistance.
drafts.baseline: Pure, equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy, whose room-temperature ductility is poor despite excellent high-temperature performance and irradiation resistance as predicted by first-principles calculations.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only for low-level Hf additions (likely ≤10 at.%) that preserve the single-phase BCC structure. Exceeding this range or choosing elements with lower melting points may lead to phase separation or deterioration of high-temperature performance and irradiation resistance.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbMoTaW alloys with varying Hf contents (e.g., 0, 2, 5, and 8 at.%) ensuring homogeneous, single-phase BCC structure via controlled annealing. Conduct tensile tests at room temperature and at 1600 °C. Subject samples to irradiation (using controlled ion or neutron irradiation experiments) while monitoring microstructural evolution.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile stress-strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility/elongation)
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM, XRD) to check for phase stability pre- and post-irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Hf does not lead to a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (as measured by increased elongation and lower yield strength) without a corresponding deterioration in high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance (compared consistently against the pure NbMoTaW baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified. Additionally, the emergence of secondary phases or deterioration in irradiation behavior would refute the proposed mechanism.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount (sub‐1 at%) of boron to equiatomic NbMoTaW promotes grain boundary cohesion via boron segregation, thereby enhancing room-temperature ductility without degrading high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equal‐atomic, single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW that exhibits excellent strength at ~1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a microalloying addition of boron (≤1 at%) during alloy synthesis.
drafts.conditions: The alloy will be evaluated under room-temperature loading, at high temperatures around 1600 °C, and under irradiation doses similar to those used in first-principles studies.
drafts.structural_mediator: Boron is expected to segregate to grain boundaries, increasing cohesion and possibly inducing a subtle dual-phase (or modified local chemistry) structure that retards crack nucleation and propagation at low temperatures.
drafts.mechanism: Trace B improves grain boundary cohesion by passivating high-energy sites, thereby reducing brittleness at room temperature. Since the overall BCC matrix is retained and the boron level is low, the high melting-point and diffusion‐controlled deformation mechanisms at 1600 °C are not significantly affected. Similarly, the local lattice distortion introduced by B is too minimal to alter the defect migration barriers responsible for irradiation resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the B-doped alloy is predicted to exhibit significantly increased plastic strain (improved ductility) at room temperature while retaining comparable yield strength at 1600 °C and maintaining a similar irradiation damage response.
drafts.baseline: Undoped, equiatomic NbMoTaW that is strong at high temperatures but extremely brittle at room temperature and whose irradiation resistance has been established via first-principles calculations.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only for very low (trace) boron additions; excessive B could lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases or secondary precipitates that would compromise high-temperature performance or irradiation stability. The processing must ensure a homogeneous distribution of B without large segregation beyond grain boundaries.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbMoTaW alloys via identical processing routes: one set with a trace addition of boron (e.g., 0.5 at%) and one set as control (no boron). Characterize the microstructure via TEM/SEM to verify boron segregation at grain boundaries and confirm that no deleterious secondary phases form. Then perform mechanical testing at room temperature and at ~1600 °C, and expose samples to simulated irradiation conditions (e.g., ion irradiation) to compare defect evolution.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength and creep resistance at 1600 °C
Irradiation-induced defect density via TEM and nanoindentation hardness measurements pre-/post-irradiation
Grain boundary chemistry and phase identification by Atom Probe Tomography (APT) or EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared to undoped samples, or if high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance is compromised (e.g., formation of brittle secondary phases, increased irradiation-induced degradation), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a minor (~5 at.%) substitution of Ti into the equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy will enhance room‐temperature ductility without notably compromising its excellent high‐temperature strength or irradiation resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy
drafts.intervention: Alloying with a small amount (around 5 at.%) of Ti by partially substituting one of the constituent elements
drafts.conditions: Room-temperature tensile tests for ductility improvement, high-temperature (∼1600 °C) mechanical tests for yield strength retention, and irradiation tests under relevant doses/temperatures
drafts.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion and activation of additional dislocation slip systems within the BCC lattice due to local lattice distortion from Ti addition
drafts.mechanism: Ti, a Group IV element, tends to promote ductile behavior by lowering the Peierls barrier for dislocation motion and improving grain-boundary cohesion at ambient temperatures. When added in trace amounts, it is expected to distort the BCC lattice just enough to favor additional slip systems without altering the high melting point and stable phase required for high-temperature and irradiation performance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Ti-doped NbMoTaW alloy will show a significant increase in room-temperature plasticity (i.e., higher tensile or compressive strain before fracture) while maintaining similar high-temperature yield strength and irradiation resistance compared to the untreated baseline.
drafts.baseline: Pristine equal-atomic NbMoTaW, which is mechanically robust at high temperatures (∼1600 °C) but exhibits very poor ductility at room temperature
drafts.boundary: Ti addition must remain slight (approximately ≤5 at.%) to retain the single-phase BCC structure and avoid the formation of secondary phases that could degrade high-temperature performance or irradiation stability

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using identical processing routes: one set of pristine NbMoTaW and another set with ~5 at.% Ti substituted. Subject both sets to room-temperature tensile (or compressive) testing, high-temperature (∼1600 °C) mechanical testing, and standardized irradiation exposure. Conduct microstructural analyses (e.g., XRD, TEM) to confirm phase stability.
measurements: Room-temperature ductility (expressed as plastic strain or elongation)
Irradiation-induced changes in hardness and microstructure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped NbMoTaW alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility relative to the pristine alloy or if its high-temperature yield strength or irradiation resistance is markedly degraded (e.g., by more than a tolerable threshold determined from baseline data), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
